title: Cost and Management Accounting
summary: Learn the management accountant's toolkit: cost classification and product costing, cost-volume-profit and break-even, absorption and marginal costing, budgets and variances, relevant costs for decisions, and performance measures.
audience: Accounting students, managers, entrepreneurs and finance staff

body.p: Management accounting gives managers information for planning, decisions and control, unlike financial accounting, which reports to outsiders. It starts with understanding how costs behave.

list: Direct costs can be traced to a product: materials in a chair, wages of the carpenter who makes it.
Indirect costs (overheads) are shared: factory rent, supervisors, electricity.
Variable costs change in total with activity (materials per unit); fixed costs stay the same in total within a range (rent).
Semi-variable costs have both parts, such as a phone bill with a fixed rental and call charges.
Product costs are attached to inventory; period costs (such as marketing) are expensed when incurred.

body.p: Behaviour matters for decisions. If rent is fixed, producing one more chair costs only its variable cost, not its "full" cost including a share of rent.

A chair uses R20 of materials and R12 of direct labour, and takes 3 machine hours. If annual overheads of R120 000 are spread over 8000 machine hours, the overhead absorption rate is R15 per hour, so the chair absorbs 3 x 15 = R45 of overhead. Full production cost = 20 + 12 + 45 = R77.

body.tip: Choose an absorption basis (labour hours, machine hours) that reflects what really drives the overhead.

body.p: Cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis shows how profit changes with sales volume.

list: Contribution per unit = selling price - variable cost. A product selling for R50 with a variable cost of R30 contributes R20 towards fixed costs and profit.
Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit. With fixed costs of R40 000: 40 000 / 20 = 2000 units.
Contribution margin ratio = contribution / price = 20 / 50 = 40%, so break-even revenue = 40 000 / 0.4 = R100 000.
Margin of safety: if budgeted sales are 3000 units, the margin of safety is (3000 - 2000) / 3000, about 33.3%; sales could fall by a third before losses begin.

body.p: CVP assumes constant prices and costs per unit within the relevant range and, for several products, a stable sales mix. Use it as a planning guide, then test the assumptions.

body.tip: To find the sales needed for a target profit, add the target to fixed costs before dividing by contribution per unit.

body.p: Two methods value inventory and report profit differently.

list: Absorption costing includes fixed production overheads in each unit's cost, as financial reporting standards require for inventory.
Marginal (variable) costing includes only variable costs in units; fixed production overheads are expensed in full each period.

body.p: When production equals sales, both give the same profit. When production exceeds sales, absorption costing shows higher profit, because some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory. Managers rewarded on absorption profit can be tempted to overproduce, building stock to boost reported profit, a reason many firms use marginal costing for internal reports.

Activity-based costing (ABC) assigns overheads using several cost drivers (number of set-ups, orders, inspections) instead of one rate. It gives more accurate costs when products use support activities very differently, for example small custom orders versus large standard runs.

body.tip: Ask which cost information a decision needs; reported full costs are often not the right numbers for short-term choices.

body.p: A budget is a financial plan, usually for a year, broken into months. Budgets coordinate departments, allocate resources and set targets. The sales budget usually comes first, then production, materials, labour, overheads, cash and the budgeted financial statements.

Standard costing sets expected costs per unit, then compares actual results. Suppose each unit should use 2 kg of material at R10 per kg. For 1000 units the standard is 2000 kg costing R20 000. Actually, 2100 kg were bought and used at R11 per kg, costing R23 100.

list: Material price variance = (standard price - actual price) x actual quantity = (10 - 11) x 2100 = R2100 adverse.
Material usage variance = (standard quantity - actual quantity) x standard price = (2000 - 2100) x 10 = R1000 adverse.
Total material variance = R3100 adverse, matching 23 100 - 20 000.

body.p: Variances direct attention to causes: a supplier price rise, poorer-quality material causing waste, or inexperienced staff. Flexible budgets, adjusted to the actual level of activity, give fairer comparisons than fixed budgets.

body.tip: Investigate large or repeated variances, not every small one; management time is a cost too.

body.p: For decisions, only relevant costs matter: future cash flows that differ between options. Sunk costs (already spent) and committed costs are irrelevant, however painful.

A component costs R28 per unit in variable costs to make; a supplier offers it at R35. If fixed costs would be the same either way, making saves R7 per unit. But if the factory space could instead make a product earning a higher contribution, that lost contribution (opportunity cost) must be added to the cost of making.

list: Special orders: accept if the price covers the relevant costs and does not damage normal sales or prices.
Limiting factors: when a resource such as machine hours is scarce, rank products by contribution per unit of that resource.
Closing a segment: compare the contribution lost with the fixed costs actually saved.
Non-financial factors: quality, reliability, staff and customer relationships.

body.tip: Write down which costs change between the options; ignore everything that does not.

body.p: Organisations measure divisions and managers to check strategy is working and to motivate good decisions.

list: Return on investment (ROI) = profit / capital employed. A division earning R60 000 on R400 000 of assets has ROI of 15%.
Residual income = profit - (required return x capital employed). At a 12% required return: 60 000 - 0.12 x 400 000 = R12 000.
Managers judged on ROI may reject projects that beat the company's required return but would lower their division's average ROI; residual income avoids this problem.
Profit margins, cost per unit and cash flow complete the picture.

body.p: A balanced scorecard adds customer measures (satisfaction, retention), internal process measures (quality, delivery times) and learning measures (training, innovation). In public and non-profit organisations, value for money (economy, efficiency and effectiveness) matters more than profit.

body.tip: Measure what drives future results, not only past profits, and keep the list short.
